newsitem.title: IRAQ: Iraq says it arrested two killers of Jordanian.
newsitem.headline: Iraq says it arrested two killers of Jordanian.

text.p: Iraq said on Tuesday that two killers of a Jordanian embassy driver shot in November while driving a diplomatic car on the desert highway between Baghdad and Amman had been arrested soon after the incident.
"Iraqi authorities concerned have arrested those who murdered the Jordanian national, Omar Ahmed Ali al-Subh, driver of the Jordanian embassy in Baghdad," the official Iraqi News Agency said.
It named three people accused by Iraqi authorities of the killing and said two of them, a Saudi and a Jordanian, were arrested on November 11 soon after the shooting.

"The killers are Zebn Battah Hdaij al-Rowaili who is a Saudi national, born in 1970 and from the Saudi province of Skakah. The second is Nasr Hantour Basheer al-Rowaili, a Jordanian, born in 1964 and from al-Za'tari area in Jordan...." INA said.
It said the two had confessed to the killing with a third person it named as Tarrad al-Halabi, who it said was Syrian. It gave no further details on Halabi.
INA said the three who entered Iraq illegally using a car with Saudi registration had also stolen the embassy car.
The killers were also reported in November to have taken the embassy's diplomatic bag, which contained 250 Jordanian passports and other documents.
The agency said they were also accused of smuggling heroin from Turkey to Saudi Arabia through Jordan.
Soon after the incident, the Jordanian Foreign Ministry summoned Iraq's ambassador to Amman and held the Iraqi government responsible for the shooting.

Jordan, once a close ally of Iraq, stood by its neighbour when a U.S.-led military coalition waged war to drive Baghdad's forces from Kuwait in 1991. Jordan's King Hussein later turned against President Saddam Hussein and called for change in Iraq, which is under United Nations sanctions imposed after the invasion of Kuwait.

But since a deal between Iraq and the U.N. late last year under which Iraq can sell $2 billion worth of oil over six months to pay for food and medicine, Jordan has made conciliatory gestures in an effort to mend fences.
Jordanian businessmen are seeking the government's support in lobbying for expanded business ties.
